title: Agent Q: Advanced Reasoning and Learning for Autonomous AI Agents
headline: A web agent that searches a tree of possible web pages, uses one model as both the actor that proposes clicks and the critic that grades them, and learns from both its wins and its mistakes.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in natural language tasks requiring complex reasoning, yet their application in agentic, multi-step reasoning within interactive environments remains a difficult challenge. Traditional supervised pre-training on static datasets falls short in enabling autonomous agent capabilities needed to perform complex decision-making in dynamic settings like web navigation. Previous attempts to bridge this gap through supervised fine-tuning on curated expert demonstrations often suffer from compounding errors and limited exploration data, resulting in sub-optimal policy outcomes. To overcome these challenges, we propose a framework that combines guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) search with a self-critique mechanism and iterative fine-tuning on agent interactions using an off-policy variant of the Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) algorithm. Our method allows LLM agents to learn effectively from both successful and unsuccessful trajectories, thereby improving their generalization in complex, multi-step reasoning tasks. We validate our approach in the WebShop environment, a simulated e-commerce platform, where it consistently outperforms behavior cloning and reinforced fine-tuning baseline, and beats average human performance when equipped with the capability to do online search. In real-world booking scenarios, our methodology boosts Llama-3 70B model's zero-shot performance from 18.6% to 81.7% success rate (a 340% relative increase) after a single day of data collection, and further to 95.4% with online search. We believe this represents a substantial leap forward in the capabilities of autonomous agents, paving the way for more sophisticated and reliable decision-making in real-world settings.

images.alt: An explorer stands at the top room of a downward-branching tree of pixel-art rooms, a sage-green lantern guide pointing one ink arrow toward the right branch while the room at the end of that path glows clay-orange and carries a small inked star, showing that the agent searches many possible web pages, listens to a critic that points at the promising branch, and remembers which path reached the goal.
images.caption: The agent searches a tree of possible web pages, follows a critic that points at the promising branch, and remembers which path reached the goal.

images.alt: One pixel-art wizard shown twice, on the left sketching three doorways onto the page and on the right writing rank numbers one, two, three beside the same three doors with a quill, the top-ranked door glowing clay-orange, showing that a single model plays both the actor that proposes the next clicks and the critic that grades them.
images.caption: The same model wears two hats: it proposes the candidate clicks, then ranks them to give itself process feedback.

images.alt: A branching tree of pixel-art rooms with a black ink arrow going down the left branch from the START room to a chest marked RESULT, and a curved arrow carrying a small clay-orange token back up to the start, showing the search picking a path, trying it all the way to a result, then carrying the score back up the tree.
images.caption: One search round picks a path down the tree, tries it to a result, then carries the score back up so every node above learns from the outcome.

images.alt: Two sibling pixel-art doorways at different heights share one room below, an ink brace measures the gap between them, the taller clay-orange door gets a star marked CHOSEN PATH and the shorter sage door gets a cross marked REJECTED PATH, showing that where two sibling moves differ in value by more than a threshold the better one becomes the preferred example and the worse one the rejected example for fine-tuning.
images.caption: Where two sibling moves differ enough in value, the better one becomes the preferred example and the worse one the rejected example the agent trains on.
